newsitem.title: GERMANY: German call money steady after Buba injects funds.
newsitem.headline: German call money steady after Buba injects funds.

text.p: German call money traded mostly steady at 3.05 percent on Wednesday despite the Bundesbank's generous net injection of funds at the weekly repo tender, which traders said carried no policy implications.
The bulk of trades was conducted at 3.05 percent but some banks said rates were between 3.02/03 percent compared with Tuesday's rates of 3.05/08 percent.
Earlier this morning the Bundesbank injected a net 7.9 billion marks into the market at a fixed three percent rate to replace a repo pact for 69.1 billion marks, which expires today.

Dealers said the unexpectedly large injection was likely related to an higher demand for cash in circulation and to offset the exit from the market of liquidity injected via currency swaps at the beginning of the week.

"In December the demand for cash in circulation is about eight to 10 billion marks higher than normal, and some two to three billion marks will likely leave the system on Thursday as part of the currency swaps," said one trader.
"Consequently the addition is not really all that generous and will not be able to move rates significantly lower," he added.

But dealers did admit a slight surprise that rates did not come off more after this morning's injection. They reasoned that shifts were still taking place and that some banks may be earmarking the additional funds for reserve holdings rather than filtering it back into the market.

Dealers said they expected December's minimum reserve target to be between 40 and 40.5 billion marks. Banks' holdings at the Bundesbank totalled 37.6 billion marks on Tuesday compare with 39.3 billion marks on Monday.
The monthly average was 39.0 billion marks compared with 39.6 billion marks.
The Frankfurt Interbank Overnight Average FIONA= was set at 3.06567 percent on Wednesday compared with 3.09400 percent on Tuesday.

Dealers stressed that today's move in no way signalled any policy implications ahead of Thursday's council meeting, where the market generally expects the central bank to keep its three headline rates steady.
